question_text: Dancing movements that do not result in a displacement of body posture in terms of place is known as ...... Mark Solution There are two major types of movements in dancing. These are: Locomotor movements (traveling movements): These are movements where the body travels through space from one location to another. Locomotor movements primarily use the feet for support however, the body can travel on other parts such as the hands. Non-locomotor movements (movements on-the-spot): These are movements that occur in the body parts or the whole body and do not cause the body to travel to another space. However, non-locomotor movements can be combined with locomotor movements such as a walk and arm swing.

Line notes E, G, B, D, F Mark Solution Treble Clef Staff What is a treble clef staff? A treble clef staff is a kind of musical notation used by instruments that have higher pitches. It consists of five lines and four spaces and is indicated by the presence of a treble clef symbol at the beginning of each line. How do I read treble clef notes? Reading treble clef notes requires knowing the pitch that each line and space represents. The lines on the treble clef staff represent the notes E, G, B, D, F from bottom to top. The spaces, also from bottom to top, represent the notes F, A, C, E. What is a treble clef? A treble clef is a symbol that appears at the beginning of lines of sheet music. It tells musicians what the notes of the staff represent and is actually a stylized letter G.

question_text: (c) Elements of contemporary dance, with examples [6 marks] (i) Body: The dancer's own body is the main instrument; every part, from fingers to feet, is used to shape movement. In contemporary dance the whole body is available, so a performer might isolate just the shoulder in one moment and involve the entire body in a falling roll in the next. Example: a dancer curls into a tight ball to express grief, then slowly unfolds, using the torso and limbs in sequence, to show recovery. (ii) Space: How the dancer uses the area around them. This covers levels (high, medium, low), directions (forward, backward, diagonal), pathways (straight, curved, zig-zag) and personal space (how close the dancer is to others). Example: a solo dancer moves from an upstage corner along a curving pathway to a low level centre stage, shrinking the space to pull the audience's focus inwards. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m (iii) Energy: The quality or force behind the movement: smooth versus sharp, strong versus gentle, sustained versus sudden. Changing the energy changes the feeling of the dance even when the steps are the same. Example: the same arm gesture done with soft, sustained energy feels peaceful, but done with sharp, percussive energy feels angry or urgent. question_text: (c) Elements of contemporary dance, with examples [6 marks] (i) Body: The dancer's own body is the main instrument; every part, from fingers to feet, is used to shape movement. In contemporary dance the whole body is available, so a performer might isolate just the shoulder in one moment and involve the entire body in a falling roll in the next. Example: a dancer curls into a tight ball to express grief, then slowly unfolds, using the torso and limbs in sequence, to show recovery. (ii) Space: How the dancer uses the area around them. This covers levels (high, medium, low), directions (forward, backward, diagonal), pathways (straight, curved, zig-zag) and personal space (how close the dancer is to others). Example: a solo dancer moves from an upstage corner along a curving pathway to a low level centre stage, shrinking the space to pull the audience's focus inwards. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m (iii) Energy: The quality or force behind the movement: smooth versus sharp, strong versus gentle, sustained versus sudden. Changing the energy changes the feeling of the dance even when the steps are the same. Example: the same arm gesture done with soft, sustained energy feels peaceful, but done with sharp, percussive energy feels angry or urgent. Agya Koo Nimo — Hometown: Foase, Ashanti Region. Genre: traditional folk and palm-wine highlife. Example works: Aburokyire Abrabo, Naa Densua, The Destiny of Man. Contribution: kept palm-wine highlife alive, taught Ghanaian music in schools and on international platforms, and used his songs to share Akan proverbs and values. Black Sherif — Hometown: Konongo, Ashanti Region. Genre: a mix of Afrobeats, highlife, trap and reggae. Example works: First Sermon, Kwaku the Traveller, Oil in my Head. question_text: (c) Two ways modern Ghanaian dances preserve and promote culture [6 marks] They keep Ghanaian identity visible to young people: dances like azonto, alkayida and shaku shaku grew from Ghanaian streets, so young dancers who take them up carry Ghanaian rhythm, body language and humour into their daily lives, strengthening their sense of national identity. They carry Ghanaian music and language across the world: these dances are usually performed to Ghanaian songs, often in Twi, Ga or Pidgin; when videos go viral on social media, the songs and language travel with them, exposing foreign audiences to Ghanaian culture. They adapt tradition into a modern form: many of the moves borrow from traditional dances (footwork from kpanlogo, waist movements from adowa), so performing them keeps traditional patterns alive in a shape that feels modern. They become a tool for tourism and cultural events: dance groups use them at festivals, Independence Day parades and shows for visiting tourists, turning culture into a positive economic activity. They teach teamwork and community spirit: most modern dances are group dances, so learning and performing them together builds the kind of community feeling that traditional Ghanaian dance has always encouraged. - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C: Dance Drama

question_text: (c) Two issues addressed in King Paluta's Aseda [4 marks] Gratitude and thankfulness to God: the song's title Aseda literally means "thanksgiving"; King Paluta uses the song to thank God for lifting him out of hardship and to remind listeners to be grateful for every small breakthrough. question_text: Planning a 20th Anniversary exhibition and tools for assembling artworks. 3(a) Three factors for planning a successful exhibition [9 marks] Theme and concept — Set a clear theme or message for the exhibition early so that every decision, from the artworks chosen to the posters, supports the same idea. Artwork selection — Choose pieces that match the theme and show the skill of the artists, keeping the overall display balanced in style and quality. Venue and space — Pick a place that is easy to reach, safe, and has enough wall space, lighting and ventilation to display the chosen works well. Schedule and dates — Plan the dates so there is enough time to build, install, promote and clean up without rushing. Budget and funding — Work out the expected costs and how they will be met, and allocate the money so that no area runs short. Marketing and promotion — Use posters, announcements and social media to inform your audience and draw them to the exhibition. Layout and installation — Plan where each piece will hang so that the visitor's eye moves smoothly from one work to the next. Lighting and conservation — Provide correct lighting and, where possible, control temperature and humidity to protect the works. Catalogue and documentation — Prepare a simple booklet or record of the works, artists and theme, for visitors and for future reference. Opening and programming — Plan an opening event and any side activities like artist talks. Feedback and evaluation — Collect comments from visitors so you can improve future exhibitions. Security and closing — Arrange for the safety of the works and plan a proper closing of the event. 3(b)(i) Two tools for cutting wires and papers [2 marks] Any two of: scissors, pliers, cutters or craft knives, wire strippers, trimmers, small saws. 3(b)(ii) Two tools for making holes in metals and plastics [2 marks] Any two of: drills, saws, reamers, countersinks, punches, rotary tools, nail and hammer, awls, bodkins. 3(b)(iii) Two tools for joining lead and copper [2 marks] Any two of: soldering iron, wire brush, pliers and grips, blowtorch, lead knife or cutter, riveting tools and rivets. - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

question_text: Drawing a cone with mass shading, and shading two conical objects with stippling and hatching. 1(a) Draw a cone using mass shading [5 marks] Your cone should be drawn in crayon or colour pencil and fill the space provided. Shade from dark on one side of the cone to light on the opposite side in a continuous gradation, with no visible line strokes. This gives the cone a rounded, solid appearance. Keep the tip lighter or darker consistently with the light source you imagine, and make the edge of the cone curve slightly to suggest volume. A sample rendering of a cone that has been solidly mass-shaded is shown in the figure. 1(b) Two different conical objects, stippling in Box A and hatching in Box B [10 marks] Choose any two objects that are conical in shape. Acceptable objects include: ice cream cone, funnel, bell, Christmas tree, snail shell, party hat, roof, volcano, umbrella, horn, yam mound, witch hat. In Box A, shade your drawn object using the stippling technique — build up the tone with many small dots placed close together where you want a darker area, and spread the dots apart where you want a lighter area. In Box B, shade the second object using the hatching technique — use a series of parallel lines; the closer the lines, the darker the tone. Keep the two objects different from each other and make the shaded tones clearly show the form of each object. - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Box A — sample stippled ice cream cone Box B — sample hatched witch hat D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section A — Visual Art

question_text: Prototype — produce a trial version of the possible solution. 2(d) Two types of balance; explain one [5 marks] Name any two of: symmetrical (formal) balance, asymmetrical (informal) balance, radial balance, occult balance. Sample explanation of symmetrical balance: Symmetrical balance means the visual weight on one side of a central line matches the visual weight on the other side. The centre line can be horizontal, vertical or diagonal. Objects on either side do not have to be identical, but each object on one side should match a similarly weighted object on the other side, producing a mirror-like effect that feels evenly balanced. Sample explanation of asymmetrical balance: In asymmetrical balance the elements on either side of the work are different, yet the overall arrangement still feels even. For example, one large dark element on one side might be balanced by several smaller lighter elements on the other side. Sample explanation of radial balance: The elements radiate outwards from a central point, creating a sense of movement and order. It is often seen in nature, such as a spider's web or the spokes of a wheel. Sample explanation of occult balance: A form of asymmetrical balance where the elements are arranged with no obvious mirror or centre, yet the work still feels settled. - - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m 2(e) Two precautions during production [2 marks] Read the labels on art materials to know any hazards before using them. Work in a well-ventilated area when using paints, solvents or adhesives that give off fumes. Wear gloves when handling chemicals or sharp materials. Wear a nose mask or respirator to avoid breathing in dust or fumes. Wear safety goggles to protect your eyes from splashes or debris. Keep your workspace clean, organised and well lit, and store materials safely after use. - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section A — Visual Art

question_text: Prototype — produce a trial version of the possible solution. 2(d) Two types of balance; explain one [5 marks] Name any two of: symmetrical (formal) balance, asymmetrical (informal) balance, radial balance, occult balance. Sample explanation of symmetrical balance: Symmetrical balance means the visual weight on one side of a central line matches the visual weight on the other side. The centre line can be horizontal, vertical or diagonal. Objects on either side do not have to be identical, but each object on one side should match a similarly weighted object on the other side, producing a mirror-like effect that feels evenly balanced. Sample explanation of asymmetrical balance: In asymmetrical balance the elements on either side of the work are different, yet the overall arrangement still feels even. For example, one large dark element on one side might be balanced by several smaller lighter elements on the other side. Sample explanation of radial balance: The elements radiate outwards from a central point, creating a sense of movement and order. It is often seen in nature, such as a spider's web or the spokes of a wheel. Sample explanation of occult balance: A form of asymmetrical balance where the elements are arranged with no obvious mirror or centre, yet the work still feels settled. - - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m 2(e) Two precautions during production [2 marks] Read the labels on art materials to know any hazards before using them. Work in a well-ventilated area when using paints, solvents or adhesives that give off fumes. Wear gloves when handling chemicals or sharp materials. Wear a nose mask or respirator to avoid breathing in dust or fumes. Wear safety goggles to protect your eyes from splashes or debris. Keep your workspace clean, organised and well lit, and store materials safely after use. - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section A — Visual Art

question_text: Chord members in tonic solfa, voice parts in a choir, and a Ghanaian composer. 5(a) Members of chords I, IV and V in tonic solfa [3 marks] Chord I: doh — me — soh (d m s). In C major this is C E G. Chord IV: fah — lah — doh (f l d). In C major this is F A C. Chord V: soh — te — ray (s t r). In C major this is G B D. 5(b) Three voice parts at a choral concert [6 marks] Soprano (Treble): the highest voice part, usually sung by women or young boys. It carries the main melody high above the other parts. Alto: the second-highest voice, below soprano. It is sung mostly by women with a lower voice or by men singing in a high range, and it fills in harmony under the soprano. Tenor: the second-lowest voice, sung by men with a higher male voice. It sits between alto and bass and often sings harmony to the melody. Bass: the lowest voice, sung by men with deep voices. It provides the foundation for the harmony and rhythm of the choir. 5(c) Short notes on one composer [6 marks] Ephraim Amu — Hometown: Peki (Avetile), Volta Region. Genre: Ghanaian art music, blending African and Western classical elements. Example works: Yen Ara Asase Ni, Bonwire Kente, Alegbegbe. Contribution: pioneered an African concert-music tradition, used Ghanaian languages and instruments like the atenteben in his compositions, and trained generations of musicians at Akropong, Achimota and the University of Ghana. Agya Koo Nimo — Hometown: Foase, Ashanti Region. Genre: traditional folk and palm-wine highlife. Example works: Aburokyire Abrabo, Naa Densua, The Destiny of Man. Contribution: kept palm-wine highlife alive, taught Ghanaian music in schools and on international platforms, and used his songs to share Akan proverbs and values. Black Sherif — Hometown: Konongo, Ashanti Region. Genre: a mix of Afrobeats, highlife, trap and reggae. Example works: First Sermon, Kwaku the Traveller, Oil in my Head. Contribution: speaks for young Ghanaians through his lyrics, blends local dialects with modern sounds, and carries Ghanaian music to a global audience. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C — Dance Drama

question_text: Chord members in tonic solfa, voice parts in a choir, and a Ghanaian composer. 5(a) Members of chords I, IV and V in tonic solfa [3 marks] Chord I: doh — me — soh (d m s). In C major this is C E G. Chord IV: fah — lah — doh (f l d). In C major this is F A C. Chord V: soh — te — ray (s t r). In C major this is G B D. 5(b) Three voice parts at a choral concert [6 marks] Soprano (Treble): the highest voice part, usually sung by women or young boys. It carries the main melody high above the other parts. Alto: the second-highest voice, below soprano. It is sung mostly by women with a lower voice or by men singing in a high range, and it fills in harmony under the soprano. Tenor: the second-lowest voice, sung by men with a higher male voice. It sits between alto and bass and often sings harmony to the melody. Bass: the lowest voice, sung by men with deep voices. It provides the foundation for the harmony and rhythm of the choir. 5(c) Short notes on one composer [6 marks] Ephraim Amu — Hometown: Peki (Avetile), Volta Region. Genre: Ghanaian art music, blending African and Western classical elements. Example works: Yen Ara Asase Ni, Bonwire Kente, Alegbegbe. Contribution: pioneered an African concert-music tradition, used Ghanaian languages and instruments like the atenteben in his compositions, and trained generations of musicians at Akropong, Achimota and the University of Ghana. Agya Koo Nimo — Hometown: Foase, Ashanti Region. Genre: traditional folk and palm-wine highlife. Example works: Aburokyire Abrabo, Naa Densua, The Destiny of Man. Contribution: kept palm-wine highlife alive, taught Ghanaian music in schools and on international platforms, and used his songs to share Akan proverbs and values. Black Sherif — Hometown: Konongo, Ashanti Region. Genre: a mix of Afrobeats, highlife, trap and reggae. Example works: First Sermon, Kwaku the Traveller, Oil in my Head. Contribution: speaks for young Ghanaians through his lyrics, blends local dialects with modern sounds, and carries Ghanaian music to a global audience. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C — Dance Drama

question_text: Boboobo costumes, Kpanlogo stage arrangement, a performing-art personality, and roles of dance drama. 6(a) Three costume items for Boboobo [3 marks] Any three of: handkerchiefs, scarves, head wraps, beaded necklaces, traditional cloth (kaba and slit). 6(b) Stage arrangement for Kpanlogo [3 marks] Drummers stand or sit at the back of the stage, often in a semi-circle or a straight line, with the lead (master) drummer in the middle. Dancers perform in front of the drummers, facing the audience so the audience can enjoy their facial expressions and footwork. They may occasionally interact with the drummers and singers. Singers stand behind the drummers or on the side, supporting the performance with voice and clapping. 6(c) Short notes on one performing-art personality [6 marks] Martin Owusu — Profession: Ghanaian playwright, drama lecturer and former Director of the School of Performing Arts, University of Ghana. Contribution: shaped African theatre through plays that explore politics, culture and social issues, and trained many leading Ghanaian actors. Example works: The Legend of Aku Sika, The Sudden Return, The Story Ananse Told, The Adventures of Sasa and Esi. Francis Nii Yartey — Profession: choreographer, dancer and artistic director; headed the Department of Dance Studies at the University of Ghana and founded the National Dance Company of Ghana. Contribution: promoted and preserved traditional Ghanaian dance, developed contemporary African dance, and staged Ghanaian dance on international platforms. Example works: opening and closing ceremonies for CAN 2008 (26th Africa Cup of Nations) and the 2009 AFHF Hockey Africa Cup of Nations in Accra. Ama Ata Aidoo — Profession: Ghanaian author, playwright, poet and former Minister of Education. Contribution: helped pioneer African feminist literature and drama, and used her work to highlight the experiences of African women. Example works: The Dilemma of a Ghost, Anowa, Changes: A Love Story. 6(d) Three roles of dance drama in Ghanaian culture [3 marks] It entertains the community during festivals and social events. It educates the audience about history, values and moral lessons. It preserves cultural heritage by passing traditions from one generation to the next. It helps bond the community together through shared performance. It can serve religious or spiritual purposes at ceremonies. It communicates messages, news or warnings in a memorable form. - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C — Dance Drama

question_text: Grouping dances by ethnic group, describing alignment and balance, and the value of storytelling. 7(a) Group the dances by ethnic group [7 marks] EWE AKAN MOLE-DAGBANI Gahu, Gota Apatampa, Kete Bamaya, Nagla, Takai 7(b) Describe two types of dance movement [4 marks] Alignment — The correct positioning of the body so that the head, torso, hips and legs are stacked in a straight line. Good alignment lets the dancer move gracefully and avoids strain on muscles and joints. Balance — The dancer's ability to keep the body steady and under control while standing, turning, leaping or landing. A balanced dancer can stop, change direction or hold a pose without falling. 7(c) Two reasons why storytelling should still be encouraged [4 marks] It passes knowledge, history and experience from one generation to the next, keeping the culture alive. It teaches morals and life lessons in a way children easily remember. It reflects and reinforces the social values that guide the community. It promotes unity, because people gather to listen and share together. It provides entertainment that is cultural and age-appropriate. It can even support tourism by showcasing Ghanaian tradition to visitors. - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

question_text: Boboobo costumes, Kpanlogo stage arrangement, a performing-art personality, and roles of dance drama. 6(a) Three costume items for Boboobo [3 marks] Any three of: handkerchiefs, scarves, head wraps, beaded necklaces, traditional cloth (kaba and slit). 6(b) Stage arrangement for Kpanlogo [3 marks] Drummers stand or sit at the back of the stage, often in a semi-circle or a straight line, with the lead (master) drummer in the middle. Dancers perform in front of the drummers, facing the audience so the audience can enjoy their facial expressions and footwork. They may occasionally interact with the drummers and singers. Singers stand behind the drummers or on the side, supporting the performance with voice and clapping. 6(c) Short notes on one performing-art personality [6 marks] Martin Owusu — Profession: Ghanaian playwright, drama lecturer and former Director of the School of Performing Arts, University of Ghana. Contribution: shaped African theatre through plays that explore politics, culture and social issues, and trained many leading Ghanaian actors. Example works: The Legend of Aku Sika, The Sudden Return, The Story Ananse Told, The Adventures of Sasa and Esi. Francis Nii Yartey — Profession: choreographer, dancer and artistic director; headed the Department of Dance Studies at the University of Ghana and founded the National Dance Company of Ghana. Contribution: promoted and preserved traditional Ghanaian dance, developed contemporary African dance, and staged Ghanaian dance on international platforms. Example works: opening and closing ceremonies for CAN 2008 (26th Africa Cup of Nations) and the 2009 AFHF Hockey Africa Cup of Nations in Accra. Ama Ata Aidoo — Profession: Ghanaian author, playwright, poet and former Minister of Education. Contribution: helped pioneer African feminist literature and drama, and used her work to highlight the experiences of African women. Example works: The Dilemma of a Ghost, Anowa, Changes: A Love Story. 6(d) Three roles of dance drama in Ghanaian culture [3 marks] It entertains the community during festivals and social events. It educates the audience about history, values and moral lessons. It preserves cultural heritage by passing traditions from one generation to the next. It helps bond the community together through shared performance. It can serve religious or spiritual purposes at ceremonies. It communicates messages, news or warnings in a memorable form. - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C — Dance Drama

question_text: Printing cloth for a political party rally, and weaving a stole for a graduation. 2(a)(i) Most appropriate printing method [2 marks] Serigraphy (also called screen printing or silk-screen printing). 2(a)(ii) Two reasons for choosing that method [4 marks] It makes mass production easy: once the screens are ready, many pieces of cloth can be printed quickly and evenly. It is cost-effective per piece when producing large quantities like the 85,000 cloths required. It handles bold and detailed designs well, so the party's logos, colours and motifs come out sharp. It is efficient: each additional print uses less time and material than other methods such as block printing. The colours are vibrant and long-lasting, which is important for cloth that will be worn at a rally. 2(a)(iii) Three wet media for printing the cloth [3 marks] oil paint acrylic paint printing paste printing ink fabric paint dye 2(b)(i) Two sets of yarns used for the stole [2 marks] Warp yarns (also called ends). question_text: Six-point colour wheel with hatched secondary colours and stippled primary colours; then list the cool colours. 1(a) Draw and shade a six-point colour wheel [12 marks] Draw a circle and divide it into six equal sectors, alternating primary and secondary colours around the wheel. The primary colours are Red, Yellow and Blue. The secondary colours (each made by mixing two primaries) are Orange (red + yellow), Green (yellow + blue) and Violet/Purple (blue + red). Place them in this order around the wheel so that each secondary sits between the two primaries it is made from: Red → Orange → Yellow → Green → Blue → Violet/Purple. Shade the three secondary sectors (Orange, Green, Violet/Purple) using hatching: parallel straight lines; the closer the lines, the darker the area looks. Shade the three primary sectors (Red, Yellow, Blue) using stippling: many small dots; cluster the dots more tightly where you want a darker tone. Label each sector clearly with its colour name and an arrow. Mark breakdown: drawing the wheel (2), labelling the secondary colours (2), hatching the secondary colours (3), labelling the primary colours (2), stippling the primary colours (3): total 12 marks. A sample of the completed wheel is shown in the figure. - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m 1(b) Cool colours on the wheel [3 marks] The cool colours on the six-point wheel are: (i) Blue (ii) Green (iii) Violet (purple) D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section A: Visual Art

question_text: Maame Dokono's contributions, performance-space anatomy, and modern Ghanaian dances as cultural promoters. 6(a) Three contributions of Grace Omaboe (Maame Dokono) [3 marks] Promoted Ghanaian storytelling on television: she hosted and starred in By the Fireside, a long- running children's TV programme that retold Ananse and other folk stories in Akan, keeping oral tradition alive for new generations. Built a celebrated acting career: she acted in numerous Ghanaian films and stage plays, becoming one of the most recognised actresses of her generation and inspiring many younger performers. Mentored and trained younger actors: through her productions and workshops she helped groom new talent in the Ghanaian creative-arts industry. Produced cultural content in local languages: her work mostly used Akan, which helped preserve and promote the use of Ghanaian languages in the media. Engaged in public and charity work: she used her public profile for charitable causes and community engagement, serving as a role model for women in the arts. Served in public office: she took on political and public-service roles that extended her cultural advocacy beyond the screen. 6(b)(i) Three parts of the performance space [3 marks] Stage Backstage Wings Auditorium (house) Orchestra pit Apron (forestage) Dressing rooms Green room Lighting booth / Sound booth (control room) 6(b)(ii) One function of each part named in (i) [3 marks] Stage: the main acting area where all performances take place in full view of the audience. Backstage: the area behind the stage used for scenery storage, set changes and out-of-sight movement between entrances. Wings: the narrow areas at each side of the stage where performers wait, hidden from the audience, before making an entrance. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Auditorium: the space where the audience sits to watch the performance. Orchestra pit: a lowered area between the stage and audience that houses the musicians accompanying the performance. Apron: the part of the stage that projects towards the audience beyond the main curtain; used for close, direct address. Dressing rooms: where performers change into costume and put on make-up before and during the show. Green room: a lounge where performers relax and wait when they are not on stage. Lighting / sound booth: the control room from which technicians operate the lighting and sound cues. 6(c) Two ways modern Ghanaian dances preserve and promote culture [6 marks] They keep Ghanaian identity visible to young people: dances like azonto, alkayida and shaku shaku grew from Ghanaian streets, so young dancers who take them up carry Ghanaian rhythm, body language and humour into their daily lives, strengthening their sense of national identity. They carry Ghanaian music and language across the world: these dances are usually performed to Ghanaian songs, often in Twi, Ga or Pidgin; when videos go viral on social media, the songs and language travel with them, exposing foreign audiences to Ghanaian culture. They adapt tradition into a modern form: many of the moves borrow from traditional dances (footwork from kpanlogo, waist movements from adowa), so performing them keeps traditional patterns alive in a shape that feels modern. They become a tool for tourism and cultural events: dance groups use them at festivals, Independence Day parades and shows for visiting tourists, turning culture into a positive economic activity. They teach teamwork and community spirit: most modern dances are group dances, so learning and performing them together builds the kind of community feeling that traditional Ghanaian dance has always encouraged. - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C: Dance Drama

question_text: Defining dance-drama, using body parts in performance, and the elements of contemporary dance. 7(a) Explain dance-drama [3 marks] Dance-drama is a form of performance that tells a complete story using dance movements together with the elements of drama: characters, a plot, costumes, music and sometimes dialogue or mime. The dancers act out the events of the story through choreographed movement; meaning is carried by the body rather than mainly by spoken words. It combines the storytelling power of drama with the emotional and rhythmic power of dance, so the audience both follows a story and enjoys the movement. 7(b) How actors and dancers use body parts in performance [6 marks] Feet: establish rhythm and energy. Stamping feet show anger or assertiveness; soft gliding steps show calmness; running shows urgency. Arms: extend the body into space and shape emotion. Raised arms show joy or victory; wide open arms welcome; crossed arms show refusal or protection. Hands: carry detailed meaning. Pointing directs attention; clenched fists show anger or determination; open palms show honesty or pleading; waving greets or dismisses. Legs: create shape and power. Bent knees ground the dancer in traditional Ghanaian style; leaps show excitement; kneeling shows submission or prayer. Head: adds focus and attitude. Nodding shows agreement; shaking shows refusal; a tilted head shows curiosity; a lowered head shows sorrow or respect. Neck: amplifies the head's meaning. A stretched neck shows pride or alertness; a relaxed neck shows calm; a turned neck directs gaze and intention. Torso: is the emotional centre of the body. A lifted chest shows confidence; a collapsed chest shows defeat; a twisted torso shows tension or conflict; hip sways carry the rhythm in many African dances. 7(c) Elements of contemporary dance, with examples [6 marks] (i) Body: The dancer's own body is the main instrument; every part, from fingers to feet, is used to shape movement. In contemporary dance the whole body is available, so a performer might isolate just the shoulder in one moment and involve the entire body in a falling roll in the next. Example: a dancer curls into a tight ball to express grief, then slowly unfolds, using the torso and limbs in sequence, to show recovery. (ii) Space: How the dancer uses the area around them. This covers levels (high, medium, low), directions (forward, backward, diagonal), pathways (straight, curved, zig-zag) and personal space (how close the dancer is to others). Example: a solo dancer moves from an upstage corner along a curving pathway to a low level centre stage, shrinking the space to pull the audience's focus inwards. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m (iii) Energy: The quality or force behind the movement: smooth versus sharp, strong versus gentle, sustained versus sudden. Changing the energy changes the feeling of the dance even when the steps are the same. Example: the same arm gesture done with soft, sustained energy feels peaceful, but done with sharp, percussive energy feels angry or urgent. D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

question_text: Notating semibreves on the treble and bass staves, classifying Western instruments, and interpreting King Paluta's Aseda. 4(a) Notate F, C (treble) and C (bass) using semibreves [6 marks] A semibreve (whole note) is written as an open (hollow) note head with no stem. Treble staff: the five lines from bottom to top spell E G B D F (mnemonic: "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit") and the four spaces spell F A C E. (i) F on a line in the treble clef is written on the very top line of the staff. (ii) C on a space in the treble clef is written in the third space from the bottom (the C of F-A-C-E). Bass staff: the five lines from bottom to top spell G B D F A ("Good Boys Deserve Fruit Always") and the four spaces spell A C E G ("All Cows Eat Grass"). (iii) C on a space in the bass clef is written in the second space from the bottom (the C of A-C-E- G). Begin each staff with the correct clef sign before drawing the semibreve on the required line or space. 2 marks per correctly placed note. 4(b) Classify the Western instruments [5 marks] Quick check: woodwinds produce sound by a vibrating reed or an edge of air (clarinet); brass by the player's buzzing lips into a metal mouthpiece (trombone); percussion by being struck (cymbals); strings by bowing or plucking taut strings (cello); electronic by generating or amplifying sound electrically (keyboard/synthesiser). WOODWINDS BRASS PERCUSSION STRINGS ELECTRONIC Clarinet Trombone Cymbals Cello Keyboard 4(c) Two issues addressed in King Paluta's Aseda [4 marks] Gratitude and thankfulness to God: the song's title Aseda literally means "thanksgiving"; King Paluta uses the song to thank God for lifting him out of hardship and to remind listeners to be grateful for every small breakthrough. Hard work and perseverance through poverty: he recounts years of struggle, rejection and financial hardship before success came, encouraging young people not to give up on their dreams. The value of family support: he acknowledges his mother and loved ones who stood by him, highlighting the importance of family in an individual's rise. Humility despite success: he warns that wealth and fame should not change a person's character, a common message in Ghanaian moral teaching. Faith and trust in God: the song frames success as God's doing and calls on listeners to put their trust in God rather than in people alone. - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

question_text: Maame Dokono's contributions, performance-space anatomy, and modern Ghanaian dances as cultural promoters. 6(a) Three contributions of Grace Omaboe (Maame Dokono) [3 marks] Promoted Ghanaian storytelling on television: she hosted and starred in By the Fireside, a long- running children's TV programme that retold Ananse and other folk stories in Akan, keeping oral tradition alive for new generations. Built a celebrated acting career: she acted in numerous Ghanaian films and stage plays, becoming one of the most recognised actresses of her generation and inspiring many younger performers. Mentored and trained younger actors: through her productions and workshops she helped groom new talent in the Ghanaian creative-arts industry. Produced cultural content in local languages: her work mostly used Akan, which helped preserve and promote the use of Ghanaian languages in the media. Engaged in public and charity work: she used her public profile for charitable causes and community engagement, serving as a role model for women in the arts. Served in public office: she took on political and public-service roles that extended her cultural advocacy beyond the screen. 6(b)(i) Three parts of the performance space [3 marks] Stage Backstage Wings Auditorium (house) Orchestra pit Apron (forestage) Dressing rooms Green room Lighting booth / Sound booth (control room) 6(b)(ii) One function of each part named in (i) [3 marks] Stage: the main acting area where all performances take place in full view of the audience. Backstage: the area behind the stage used for scenery storage, set changes and out-of-sight movement between entrances. Wings: the narrow areas at each side of the stage where performers wait, hidden from the audience, before making an entrance. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Auditorium: the space where the audience sits to watch the performance. Orchestra pit: a lowered area between the stage and audience that houses the musicians accompanying the performance. Apron: the part of the stage that projects towards the audience beyond the main curtain; used for close, direct address. Dressing rooms: where performers change into costume and put on make-up before and during the show. Green room: a lounge where performers relax and wait when they are not on stage. Lighting / sound booth: the control room from which technicians operate the lighting and sound cues. 6(c) Two ways modern Ghanaian dances preserve and promote culture [6 marks] They keep Ghanaian identity visible to young people: dances like azonto, alkayida and shaku shaku grew from Ghanaian streets, so young dancers who take them up carry Ghanaian rhythm, body language and humour into their daily lives, strengthening their sense of national identity. They carry Ghanaian music and language across the world: these dances are usually performed to Ghanaian songs, often in Twi, Ga or Pidgin; when videos go viral on social media, the songs and language travel with them, exposing foreign audiences to Ghanaian culture. They adapt tradition into a modern form: many of the moves borrow from traditional dances (footwork from kpanlogo, waist movements from adowa), so performing them keeps traditional patterns alive in a shape that feels modern. They become a tool for tourism and cultural events: dance groups use them at festivals, Independence Day parades and shows for visiting tourists, turning culture into a positive economic activity. They teach teamwork and community spirit: most modern dances are group dances, so learning and performing them together builds the kind of community feeling that traditional Ghanaian dance has always encouraged. - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C: Dance Drama

question_text: Observational drawing of fruit with three shading techniques, then identifying and drawing a line in nature. 1(a)(i) Three bananas in mass shading [4 marks] Draw a bunch of three bananas in correct proportion and overlapping naturally. Render in three tones (light, medium, dark) using mass shading: lay down solid tone and blend smoothly so no separate lines or dots show. Show the light source: lightest tone where light hits, darkest tone on the shadow side, medium tone between. Mark guide: drawing the bananas (1), three clear tones (2), smooth mass-shading technique (1). 1(a)(ii) An orange in hatching [4 marks] Draw a single round orange in good proportion. Render in three tones using hatching: sets of parallel lines; place the lines closer together for darker areas and further apart for lighter areas. Keep the lines following the round form of the orange so it looks solid. Mark guide: drawing the orange (1), three clear tones (2), correct hatching technique (1). 1(a)(iii) Composition of both objects in stippling [4 marks] Arrange the bananas and the orange together in one balanced composition, overlapping for depth. Render in three tones using stippling: many small dots; cluster the dots tightly for dark areas and spread them out for light areas. Keep one consistent light source across both objects. Mark guide: composing the objects (1), three clear tones (2), correct stippling technique (1). 1(b)(i) A natural object that is an example of a line [1 mark] Any natural object seen as a line, for example: the stem or branch of a plant, the veins of a leaf, blades of grass, a tree root, a spider's web thread, a crack in the ground, or the horizon. 1(b)(ii) Draw the example [2 marks] Make a clear, simple drawing of the object named in (b)(i), showing its line-like quality (length and direction). - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section A: Visual Art

question_text: Features of art music, notes in a 3/4 bar, conducting pattern and triads. 4(a) State and explain two features of art music [4 marks] It is composed and written down (notated) by a known composer using staff notation, so it can be performed exactly as written. It is performed from a score, usually by trained musicians who follow the composer's instructions on pitch, rhythm and dynamics. It uses Western harmony, form and instruments such as the choir, organ or orchestra. It is usually performed in formal concert settings (for example by choirs and orchestras), for example anthems, hymns and cantatas. 4(b)(i) A different set of notes that fit a 3/4 bar [3 marks] The time signature is 3/4, so each bar must add up to three crotchet beats. Any correct combination totalling three crotchet beats is accepted, for example: a dotted minim (3 beats); a minim + a crotchet (2 + 1); a crotchet + four quavers (1 + 2) ... continue to total 3; six quavers (½ × 6 = 3). The set drawn must be different from the one given in the question. 4(b)(ii) Suitable conducting pattern for 3/4 [2 marks] Use the three-beat (triangular) conducting pattern. The hand moves down on beat 1, out to the right on beat 2, and up back to the start on beat 3 (down – out – up), forming a triangle. 4(c)(i) Triad with C as root, treble clef [3 marks] A triad is the root, the third above it and the fifth above the root, played together. On C the triad is C – E – G; notate these three notes stacked on the treble staff (C, the E a third above, the G a fifth above). question_text: a. i. Identify the topologies labelled A, B, C and D A - Hybrid topology B - Tree topology C - Ring topology D - Dual ring topology             1 mark each × 4 = 4 marks ii. State one feature each of the diagrams labelled above. A - Hybrid Topology * Combination: Utilizes a mixture of two or more different network topologies. * Scalability: Offers flexibility for expansion and adaptation to varying network requirements. * Reliability: Provides redundancy and fault tolerance by incorporating multiple topology structures. * Complexity: Can be more complex to design, implement, and manage compared to single- topology networks. B - Tree Topology: * Hierarchy: Organized in a hierarchical structure with a root node at the top and branches extending downward. * Centralization: Features a central node (root) that controls the flow of communication. * Scalability: Supports expansion by adding more branches or nodes to the existing structure. * Dependency: Relies heavily on the central node, making it vulnerable to single point of failure. C - Ring Topology: * Ring Structure: Nodes are connected in a circular arrangement, where each node is connected to exactly two other nodes. * Token Passing: Utilizes token passing mechanism for data transmission, where only the node with the token can send data. * Simple Configuration: Relatively simple to configure and implement compared to other topologies. * Failure Impact: Susceptible to network disruption if any node or connection in the ring fails, causing the entire network to be affected. D - Dual Ring Topology: * Redundancy: Features two interconnected rings, providing redundancy and fault tolerance. * Data Transmission: Utilizes one ring for data transmission while the other serves as a backup. * Increased Reliability: Offers increased reliability compared to a single ring topology due to redundancy. * Complexity: Can be more complex to implement and manage compared to single-ring topologies due to dual infrastructure. 1 mark each × any 4 = 4 marks b. i. Give three functions of the transport layer in the Open System Interconnection (OSI) model. * Segmentation and reassembly: Breaking data into smaller units for transmission and reassembling them at the destination. * Error detection and correction: Identifying and correcting errors that may occur during data transmission. * Flow control: Regulating the flow of data between sender and receiver to prevent congestion and ensure smooth transmission. * Multiplexing: Managing multiple data streams over a single network connection by assigning unique identifiers to each stream. * Connection establishment and termination: Setting up and tearing down communication sessions between sender and receiver. 2 mark each × 3 = 6 marks iv. Define information security. refers to the practice of protecting information and data from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction. 2 marks v.
